title: What is strange about the path of the ball?
description: A ball rolls down slope after slope, and the path comes back to its start. The board adds up the drops, compares them with the height at the start, and shows how the drawing on the grid hides the break.
teaching_notes: One idea: a path that goes down at every step cannot return to its start height in real space, and a flat drawing can hide this because a near point and a far point land on the same spot. Watch for students who trust the picture over the heights.

video_script.why: The child spots an impossible path by adding up the drops and sees how a flat drawing can hide the break.
video_script.substitution: Add up the drops along the path and compare the total with the change in height from the start back to the start.
video_script.anchor: a ball rolling down four slopes that seem to form a closed loop, drawn on a grid
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, the ball keeps going down yet comes back to its start, which is impossible in real space

final_answer.value: Yes: the ball keeps going down yet comes back to its start, which is impossible in real space
final_answer.spoken: yes, the ball keeps going down yet comes back to its start, which is impossible in real space

hold_back: Answer: Yes: the ball keeps going down yet comes back to its start, which is impossible in real space
never_show: a ball path that rises marked as the answer
maths_rules: stand-in path: 4 slopes, each taking the ball 1 unit down
back at the start the ball is at its first height, so the change in height is 0
4 units lower and 0 units lower cannot both be true in real space
on the isometric grid a near point and a far point can land on the same spot
video_script.design: A ball rolls along four slopes drawn on the stage. A height ruler beside it counts the drops, then the loop is redrawn from the side to show that the ends do not meet.
open_questions: The ball path of the book is a picture that is not in the extracted text, so the video uses a loop of four slopes that each drop one unit, which stands for the pictured path.
